title: Establish an area of turf with grass sods

lessons.title: Preparing the soil for sods
lessons.html:
Preparing the soil for sods

Grass sods (also called turf or instant lawn) are pieces or rolls of growing grass cut with a thin layer of soil. Common lawn grasses in South Africa are kikuyu, LM grass, Cynodon (quick grass) types, buffalo grass and some cool-season grasses in shady areas. Good soil preparation is the most important part of the job. Sods laid on poor ground will die, sink or stay bumpy for years.

Steps to prepare the area

  1. Mark out the area with pegs and string, following the plan.
  2. Remove what is there: old grass, weeds, roots, stones, building rubble and rubbish. Pull out weeds with roots, especially kikuyu runners and nut grass if the new lawn is a different grass.
  3. Loosen the soil with a fork, spade or rotavator, to about the depth set by your supervisor. Compacted soil stops roots from growing.
  4. Add compost and fertiliser as the plan or your supervisor says, and mix it into the top soil.
  5. Level the soil: rake it smooth. Fill hollows and remove humps. Make a gentle slope away from buildings so water runs off.
  6. Firm the soil: walk over it or roll it lightly, then rake again. This stops sods from sinking later.
  7. Set the level: the soil must be a sod's thickness below paths, edges and paving, so the finished lawn is flush.
  8. Water lightly the day before or just before laying, so the soil is moist but not muddy.

Ordering and receiving sods

  • Measure the area in square metres (length x width) and add a little extra for cutting.
  • Lay sods on the day they arrive. Sods in a stack heat up and turn yellow.
  • Keep stacks in the shade and keep them moist if there is a delay.
  • Check that sods are green, healthy, free of weeds and of even thickness.

lessons.title: Laying, watering and caring for new turf
lessons.html:
Laying the sods

  1. Start along a straight edge, such as a path or a string line.
  2. Lay the first row end to end, with joints pushed tightly together. No gaps, no overlaps.
  3. Lay the next row with joints staggered, like bricks in a wall. This makes the lawn stronger.
  4. Work from a plank laid on the sods you have already laid, so you do not make footprints in the prepared soil.
  5. Cut sods to fit curves and edges with a sharp spade or knife. Avoid small pieces at the edges; they dry out. Put full sods at the edge and small pieces inside.
  6. On slopes, lay sods across the slope and peg them down with wooden pegs if needed.
  7. Fill any small gaps with fine soil or top dressing.
  8. Roll or tamp the area lightly so roots touch the soil.

Watering

  • Water straight away after laying, before the sods dry out. Water well enough that the soil under the sod gets wet. Lift a corner to check.
  • Keep the sods moist every day for the first weeks, as your supervisor instructs. Water early in the morning.
  • As roots grow into the soil, water less often but more deeply.
  • Watch the edges and slopes. They dry out first.

Aftercare

  • Keep people and animals off the lawn until the roots hold. Test by lifting a corner gently; when it holds, the roots have grown in.
  • First cut: when the grass has grown and the roots hold, cut with a sharp mower set high.
  • Fertilise later as the maintenance plan says.
  • Pull out any weeds that come up.

Safety

  • Lift sods and rolls with bent knees and straight back. Wet sods are heavy.
  • Wear gloves and boots.
  • Only trained workers use the rotavator or roller. Keep feet clear of blades.
  • Use sunscreen, a hat and drink water.

Key points

  • Good soil preparation is the key to a good lawn.
  • Remove weeds and rubble, loosen, add compost, level and firm the soil.
  • Lay sods on the day of delivery with tight, staggered joints.
  • Work from a plank and water at once after laying.
  • Keep the new lawn moist and keep traffic off until roots hold.
